title: The Lion, the Fox and the Calf
intro: A lion sees a fat calf and sends a fox to fetch him, on pain of losing his own head. Shawqi gives most of the story to the fox, who invents a vacancy at court and a personal grievance only the new minister can redress. The size of the candidate’s head becomes his chief qualification. By the end the fox has very different reasons for valuing a head.

translation: The lion cast an eye on a fine fat calf
in the safety of a field close by.
1.sharh: The field is safe from the calf’s point of view. The lion need only look across to it for that assurance to grow doubtful.

translation: The ruler had a taste for his flesh.
So precious things beguile the heart.
2.sharh: A maxim about the attractions of rare things lends dignity to a craving for meat. Calling the hungry animal the ruler prepares the way for the fox’s tale of high office.

translation: “Master of ruses,” he told the fox,
“your precious head or that gazelle.”
3.sharh: The “gazelle” is the calf the lion has just seen. One of two heads will pay for his appetite, and the fox’s cleverness has suddenly become a matter of survival.

translation: He wished his master fortune and long life
and left at once on his momentous errand.
4.sharh: A threat receives a courtier’s blessing in reply. Procuring supper takes on the language of an affair of state.

translation: He came to the field when darkness had fallen,
found the calf and offered him peace.
5.sharh: Peace is the fox’s first offering. The reader already knows the terms on which the visitor himself has come.

translation: “My lord minister,” he said,
“you have mercy and kindness to spare.
6.sharh: The appointment is slipped into the greeting as an accomplished fact. The praise also tells the calf what kind of minister he is expected to be.

translation: Envy drove the wolf to seek my death.
He informed against me to our lord the lion.
7.sharh: The wolf enters the story only through the fox’s accusation. A dangerous visitor now has a part he can play as an injured petitioner.

translation: I have thrown myself on your high standing,
the surest advocate we know.”
8.sharh: Rank itself becomes an intercessor. No proof of the appointment has been offered, yet the calf is already being asked to exercise its privileges.

translation: The dupe wept for the rogue’s plight
and drew near to hear the whole story.
9.sharh: Compassion makes the calf take a step closer of his own accord. The narrator calls one animal the dupe and the other the rogue while they are drawing together.

translation: “Surely, sweet-natured one, you have heard
our master, the father of elephants, is dead.
10.sharh: The vacant post now gets a former holder. The fox treats the calf’s ignorance as a surprise, an economical way of making a made-up death sound like common knowledge.

translation: The sultan saw in a great head
a home for wisdom and uncommon skill.
11.sharh: The elephant’s most visible qualification can pass straight to the calf. Nobody needs to ask what either animal has ever done.

translation: He sees in you the choicest of ministers,
a pillar held in reserve for the realm.
12.sharh: The language of office piles up. In Arabic the fox now addresses the calf in the honorific plural, letting him hear what it sounds like to be important.

translation: Among your ancestors, they tell us,
are Apis and the calf the Israelites worshipped.
13.sharh: The Egyptian sacred bull and the golden calf from the story of Moses supply an absurd pedigree. Both connections depend on the candidate looking like the object of reverence.

translation: They have set a throne for Your Excellency
at the right hand of the mighty king.
14.sharh: The position of the seat makes the promotion tangible. The calf can already picture where he will sit in relation to the king.

translation: The birds and beasts stand ready,
awaiting their exalted lord there.
15.sharh: An audience is conjured up to fill the room around the throne. Keeping so many creatures waiting would make declining the honour positively discourteous.

translation: Once you shoulder the burdens of office
and find all joy and gladness yours,
16.sharh: The fox allows a line for the calf to enjoy high office in anticipation. The unfinished sentence holds his own request back a little longer.

translation: clear my name before the lord of our age.
Ask him to pardon me and keep me safe.
17.sharh: The request for protection is perfectly sincere in one respect. The fox’s life really is in danger, and the calf alone does not know the price of his safety.

translation: Enough that I am your obedient servant.
I serve my benefactor with all the strength I have.”
18.sharh: The fox offers service in return for patronage. He has arranged things so neatly that the intended victim now feels responsible for the visitor.

translation: The calf sharpened his horns and said,
“From this day you are under my protection. None shall touch you.
19.sharh: Sharpening his horns makes a fine show of readiness. Under the custom of protection, taking someone as a neighbour also meant undertaking to defend him.

translation: Go on, show me the way to the lion.
No friend ever comes to grief there through me.”
20.sharh: The calf has to ask for directions to the court over which he expects to wield influence. He is now urging his own escort to hurry.

translation: Off went the two friends, straight into the waste,
one towards death and one towards life.
21.sharh: The two pronouns send the companions in opposite directions while they walk side by side. The calf leaves behind the safe field of the opening.

translation: There the lion swallowed the minister
and gave the fox a little of him.
22.sharh: The calf keeps his courtesy title right up to the moment of being eaten. The fox’s reward comes from his supposed benefactor in a particularly literal way.

translation: He turned away laughing at the folly of calves
and entered the lists of boasting with these words,
23.sharh: An individual victim becomes a whole class of fools in the survivor’s telling. The image of a racecourse gives the fox an audience for his victory lap.

translation: “A small head brought the fox out safe.
Let every great head pay his ransom.”
24.sharh: The small head is the one the lion initially demanded. The fox closes by giving the great head a second value, the price of getting his own back intact.

1.1.2.head: اللَّيث
1.1.2.meaning: A lion, a word associated with prowess before the animal is styled a ruler.

1.2.4.head: غَيط
1.2.4.meaning: A cultivated field, a familiar word in the Egyptian countryside.

1.2.5.meaning: Secure or sheltered, applied to the calf’s field.

2.2.3.head: أَصبى
2.2.3.meaning: Beguiled, roused a longing for something.

2.2.4.meaning: Something prized or eagerly desired. The lion has his eye on meat.

3.1.4-5.head: ذو الاِحتِيال
3.1.4-5.meaning: “Master of ruses”, the fox’s particular qualification for the errand.

3.2.1.head: رَأس
3.2.1.meaning: Head in the sense of life itself, what the fox will forfeit if he fails.

3.2.5.meaning: A gazelle. The lion uses the name of game for the calf in sight. Hindawi prints ghazal, without the second long vowel.

4.1.2.head: السَّعد
4.1.2.meaning: Good fortune, one of the conventional wishes for a ruler.

4.2.5.meaning: Of great moment, the high official register in which the errand is described.

5.1.4-5.meaning: “The dark covered everything”, night had closed in.

6.1.4.meaning: Lord or patron, a flattering title for someone whose favour is sought.

6.2.4.head: البِرّ
6.2.4.meaning: Active kindness or generosity, a virtue the fox wants his addressee to feel obliged to display.

7.1.5.meaning: Envy is the delayed subject of “drove”. In the fox’s story it made the wolf act.

7.2.1.head: وَشى
7.2.1.meaning: Informed against someone, hoping to bring down the ruler’s anger on him.

8.1.1.head: تَرامى
8.1.1.meaning: Threw himself on someone’s mercy as a suppliant.

8.2.6.meaning: An intercessor who pleads another’s cause before someone in power.

9.1.2.head: المَغرور
9.1.2.meaning: The dupe, someone taken in by appearances.

9.2.1.head: دَنا
9.2.1.meaning: Drew close, the calf’s first voluntary move towards his captor.

10.2.3-4.head: أَبو الأَفيال
10.2.3-4.meaning: “Father of elephants”, the supposedly deceased holder of the ministry.

11.2.1.head: مَوطِن
11.2.1.meaning: A dwelling or seat. The fox asks the calf to imagine that wisdom needs a large head to live in.

11.2.3.head: الحِذق
11.2.3.meaning: Skill or deftness acquired in doing something well.

12.1.4.head: اِستَوزَرَ
12.1.4.meaning: Appointed someone minister, used here of the person appointed.

12.2.3.head: رُكن
12.2.3.meaning: A supporting pillar, someone on whom the state can lean.

13.2.2.head: آبيس
13.2.2.meaning: Apis, the sacred bull worshipped at Memphis in ancient Egypt.

13.2.3-4.head: مَعبود اليَهود
13.2.3-4.meaning: The golden calf worshipped by some of the Israelites during Moses’ absence. The fox presses this particular episode into service as family history.

14.1.2.head: مَعالٍ
14.1.2.meaning: “Your Excellency”, an honorific used of high officials.

14.1.3.meaning: A throne or seat of honour beside the king.

14.2.2.head: يَمين
14.2.2.meaning: The king’s right hand, a place of favour in the imagined court.

15.1.3.head: الوَحش
15.1.3.meaning: Wild land animals, distinguished from the birds in the assembled crowd.

15.2.4.meaning: High or exalted. The a before l is long in the honorific the fox holds out to the calf.

16.1.3.head: أَعباء
16.1.3.meaning: Burdens, the responsibilities that come with office.

16.2.2.head: الأُنس
16.2.2.meaning: Convivial pleasure in company, among the promised attractions of office.

17.1.1.head: بَرَّأَ
17.1.1.meaning: Cleared someone of a charge. The fox gives his request the plural of respect.

18.2.2.head: المُنعِم
18.2.2.meaning: A benefactor or patron on whose bounty one depends.

18.2.3-4.head: جُهد المُستَطيع
18.2.3-4.meaning: “The utmost a man can do”. The fox pledges every bit of strength at his disposal.

19.1.1.head: أَحَدَّ
19.1.1.meaning: Sharpened or whetted, here the tips of the horns.

19.2.4.head: جار
19.2.4.meaning: A person under another’s protection, entitled to more than the ordinary courtesies of a neighbour.

20.2.4.meaning: In the lion’s presence. The calf claims his own influence will protect his friend there.

21.1.2.head: الخِلّان
21.1.2.meaning: Two close friends, an ironic name for this pair of travelling companions.

21.1.4.head: الفَلاة
21.1.4.meaning: The open waste or wilderness beyond the cultivated field.

22.2.1.head: حَبا
22.2.1.meaning: Bestowed as a favour from a ruler.

22.2.4.head: اليَسير
22.2.4.meaning: A small portion, the lion’s reward paid out of the kill.

23.1.4.head: طَيش
23.1.4.meaning: Rashness, the failure to stop and consider.

23.2.3-4.head: حَلبَة الفَخر
23.2.3-4.meaning: “The racecourse of boasting”, an arena for competing claims to glory.

24.2.1.head: فَدى
24.2.1.meaning: Paid a ransom or gave a life in exchange for another.

24.2.4-5.head: رَأس كَبير
24.2.4-5.meaning: “A great head”. The size of the calf’s head still carries the false promise of political eminence.
